questions_and_answers.question: What kinds of figurative language does King use in his speech to describe inequality and the work of the Civil Rights Movement? What is the impact of this language? Explain examples from at least two different paragraphs of the speech.
questions_and_answers.answer: Answers will vary; students should identify metaphors from at least two paragraphs of the text. Students could discuss how King compares the "Negro's legitimate discontent" with a "sweltering summer" in paragraph 7. King emphasizes the oppression that African Americans face in America due to discrimination and segregation. He also states that this oppressive summer "will not pass until there is an invigorating autumn of freedom and equality." King's comparison draws attention to the relief and change the nation will experience as African Americans gain access to their civil rights. Students could discuss King's description of the Civil Rights movement as a "whirlwinds of revolt." This word choice suggests the energy and strength of the movement. In paragraph 19, King again compares oppression to heat and describes transforming Mississippi into an "oasis" of freedom, a place that is cool and peaceful. In paragraph 24, he describes his dream as the reshaping of the earth, using language from the Bible: "every valley shall be exalted," or lifted up, and "every hill and mountain shall be made low," or changed into flat land. This reshaping of the earth is a metaphor for bringing equality between all groups of people. Students should also identify that this figurative language emphasizes the dramatic changes the Civil Rights movement can bring. By using metaphors that compare the movement to the earth and nature, King communicates the significance of the fight for equal rights.
